summary:
The Manitoba Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and accommodation. On 18 March 2025 the provincial government introduced a bill to add gender expression as a protected ground; Justice Minister Matt Wiebe stated the change would bring Manitoba into line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The bill was before the Legislative Assembly for debate later in 2025, and Trans Manitoba executive director Charlie Eau welcomed it.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police in Canada recorded 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, a 1% increase over 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba recorded the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000, alongside Newfoundland and Labrador, with no increase in 2024; it was one of eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations in that data was published by Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation. Police-reported figures capture only incidents reported to police.

On 30 May 2024 the Manitoba legislature passed a bill recognising 31 March as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.

On 20 November 2023 the province raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance first marked eight years earlier. The flag was raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara stated that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing.

Changing the gender marker on vital statistics documents, including birth certificates, falls under provincial jurisdiction in Canada; transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been interpreted to include transsexuality and applies to all laws and government institutions, including law enforcement, with courts required to interpret human rights statutes consistently with the Charter.
tangentialFactors:
Provincial legislative activity on trans rights in Canada has moved in both directions. Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 in 2023, invoking the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity; this prompted human rights calls for repeal and legal action. Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to prevent Alberta court challenges. Manitoba's own trajectory, by contrast, has been toward added recognition, including the 31 March visibility day and the pending gender-expression amendment.

In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologised for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against homophobia, transphobia and marginalisation, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and discrimination in practices and policies.

A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported that 87.6% said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person; 91.8% said they would be comfortable if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. Canada ranked first in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024.
localsOnly:
Manitoba's Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and accommodation, giving residents a provincial complaint route on that ground. The 18 March 2025 bill to add gender expression would extend that protection to preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing; as of that reporting it was in the legislature awaiting debate later in 2025, and its final status is not documented in this record.

Residents can change the gender marker on Manitoba vital statistics documents, including birth certificates, under provincial rules; the specific Manitoba procedure and evidentiary requirements are not detailed in this inventory.

Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature, represents Kirkfield Park and brought forward the Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility bill passed on 30 May 2024. Trans Manitoba, whose executive director is Charlie Eau, is an active provincial advocacy organisation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The final status of the gender-expression amendment bill introduced on 18 March 2025 is unresolved in this record; whether it passed, was amended, or remained pending after the 2025 debate is not sourced here.

Manitoba's specific rules and evidentiary requirements for changing a gender marker on birth certificates and other vital statistics documents are not sourced in this inventory; only the general provincial jurisdiction over vital statistics is documented.

The Statistics Canada hate-crime figures for 2024 are not broken down by motivation category in this inventory for Manitoba specifically, so the province's rate cannot be attributed to gender-identity-motivated incidents. Police-reported data capture only incidents reported to police.

No Manitoba-specific incident of violence against a trans person, with date and outcome, is documented in this inventory; the 20 November 2023 Remembrance Day statements describe transphobic violence generally without a Manitoba case.
